source.title: LensLLM: Unveiling Fine-Tuning Dynamics for LLM Selection
source.authors: Xin-Yue Zeng; Hao-Hui Wang; Jun-Hong Lin; Jun Wu; Tyler Cody; Da-Wei Zhou

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. The body identifies proceedings of ICML 2025, while the supplied venue metadata says ICDMW 2025; the text also contains apparent typographical or mathematical inconsistencies.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies fine-tuning loss scaling and argues for distinct pre-power and power phases, refining a single-law account in this setting. It also reports test-loss prediction comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fine-tuning loss prediction RMSEs in Table 2 and describes a pre-power-to-power transition in Figure 2. Table 3's model-selection correlations, efficiency results, and hyperparameter sensitivity tables do not directly measure the claim versions and are not recorded as rows. The paper's pretraining scaling-law description and citations are not its own pretraining results.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a model-selection method paper. Its only result bearing on a claim version is the Figure 2 description: fine-tuning test loss against training-set size shows a 'pre-power phase' at small D before a power phase. The paper backs this with a PAC-Bayesian argument (Remarks 1–3). That is a specific argument that the power-law form in fine-tuning holds only after a transition, which bears on V5 and V7. Table 2 RMSEs compare the authors' own predictor (LensLLM) with a competing fit (Rectified Scaling Law). They measure the study's method against another method, not whether loss follows a power law, so they should not be result rows for any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors derive a PAC-Bayesian bound that, they argue, explains distinct pre-power and power phases in fine-tuning. On that basis they propose LensLLM, an NTK-based rectified scaling model. They report that it beats five baselines for LLM selection (up to 85.8% PearCorr and 91.1% RelAcc on Gigaword) and cuts compute by up to 88.5% versus FullTuning. Their claim is about the selection method; they do not claim to test pretraining scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: This study concerns supervised fine-tuning loss as training-set size changes, using an NTK-based rectified model and comparisons with another fine-tuning scaling model. It does not reproduce the original pretraining sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that prediction method changes RMSE. It also reports sensitivity analyses for stopping thresholds, learning rate, batch size, and input length, but those outcomes concern model-selection metrics rather than the scaling-law versions cataloged here.

fits_no_version.finding: The LensLLM rectified form, L(D)=B/(F(Θ,t)+D^β)+E, fits fine-tuning test loss across data sizes for 14 models and 3 datasets. Its RMSE is about 0.017–0.036, against 0.087–0.15 for Rectified Scaling Law (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A rectified power law with an NTK-based pretraining term describes fine-tuning loss against data size more accurately than earlier fine-tuning scaling laws.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW), per supplied metadata; the paper body also identifies ICML 2025 proceedings.
record.problems: The paper does not report uncertainty intervals for Table 2. The scaling experiment is on fine-tuning rather than pretraining, and the reported prediction errors do not establish the claimed orders-of-magnitude extrapolation. The theoretical phase discussion is not accompanied by numeric phase-transition estimates in the supplied text. The paper text has inconsistencies, including conflicting venue identification.
record.rows_left_out: None of the directly relevant Table 2 model–dataset RMSE comparisons or the Figure 2 phase description were left out. Other results, including Table 3 selection metrics and Tables 4–11 efficiency and sensitivity measurements, do not directly test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining-loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger. Table 2 is a fit-method comparison over fine-tuning data sizes (200 to 1.6M examples).
No controlled depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Only supervised LM fine-tuning against data size is examined. Other modalities, repeated data and transfer are not tested.
No downstream-task performance scaling against scale or pretraining loss. Selection metrics concern ranking models.
No test of parameter counting, schedule, or effects of fitting method on exponents or compute-optimal splits.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence for the phase transition is a single unlabeled figure plus theory. The O(n^-3/4) pre-power term comes from a bound, not a measurement. The Table 2 rows are method-comparison values and should be relinked to none. Venue conflict: the body says ICML 2025 while the metadata says ICDMW. The values in Table 2 (×10^-1) match the text's absolute RMSEs, e.g. OPT-6.7B 0.026 vs 0.132.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
Prediction is reported for fine-tuning test loss across training-data sizes, not for pretraining runs; orders-of-magnitude extrapolation is not established.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The tested extension is supervised language-model fine-tuning over training-data size; other modalities, repeated data, and transfer regimes are not tested.
No test of downstream-task performance scaling as a function of pretraining loss or scale.
The paper describes a fine-tuning phase transition and compares prediction methods, but does not test parameter-count conventions, compute-optimal splits, or alternative exponent-fitting choices.

rows.subject: fine-tuned LLMs (aggregate; models not identified for Figure 2)
rows.operation_detail: Describes test loss as training sample size increases, with a transition from a pre-power phase to a power phase.

conditions.value: small-data regime followed by increasing sample size

rows.measure: Fine-tuning test-loss scaling behavior
rows.value: Pre-power phase at small D, followed by a power phase after a transition; no numeric values stated.
rows.note: The paper describes the figure as showing data, but gives no model identities or numeric measurements for this aggregate result.
rows.check: For V5 the state should be partial: the power law holds only after a transition, not at small D. For V7 the curve bending away from a single power law is observed. Figure 2 names no models, datasets or numbers, and the text does not say where the transition point falls, so the evidence is qualitative. A similar pre-power phase was reported earlier by Haowei et al. (2024), which this paper cites.

relationships.condition: Supervised fine-tuning of pretrained LMs, test loss against fine-tuning set size
relationships.reason: Figure 2 and §2.1 describe a pre-power phase at small D before power-law behaviour appears (phase). This is qualitative only, with no models or numbers.
relationships.display_finding: Test loss passed through an initial phase at small dataset sizes before power-law behavior emerged.

relationships.condition: Supervised fine-tuning of pretrained LMs, test loss against fine-tuning set size
relationships.reason: Fine-tuning loss curves bend from a pre-power regime into a power regime rather than following one power law (phase). This is qualitative, without numeric transition estimates.
relationships.display_finding: Loss curves transition from an initial regime into power-law scaling rather than following a single power law throughout, without numerical transition estimates.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuning test-loss prediction across the models and datasets in Table 2
reader_labels.reason: L ENS LLM has lower reported RMSE than Rectified Scaling Law in every listed model–dataset comparison (r01–r42). The results do not demonstrate orders-of-magnitude pretraining extrapolation.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuning loss as training sample size increases
reader_labels.reason: The paper describes an initial pre-power phase before the power phase, so the power-law behavior is not presented as holding uniformly across all fine-tuning data sizes (phase).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuning loss across training sample size
reader_labels.reason: The reported pre-power-to-power transition supports the qualification that curves can depart from a single power-law regime (phase).
